computation_sheet.setback_west_rationale: Drainage easement (3m) governs over standard 2.0m side setback
computation_sheet.governing_ambf_source: PSO (2,500 sqm) is MORE restrictive than setback-derived area (4,132.5 sqm)

Adequate parking for staff and visitors

hidden_traps.title: PSO Governs Over Setbacks
hidden_traps.description: For GI zones with 50% PSO on large lots, PSO-derived AMBF (2,500 sqm) is MORE restrictive than setback-derived AMBF (4,132.5 sqm). Students expecting setbacks to govern (typical for residential) will choose the wrong area.
hidden_traps.correct_concept: PSO limits building footprint; setbacks are a secondary constraint.

hidden_traps.title: High ISA Requirement for Schools
hidden_traps.description: School campuses require 30% ISA (1,500 sqm) for playgrounds, covered courts, and active recreation. Students may apply a standard 10% ISA, resulting in only 500 sqm, which is insufficient for DepEd standards.
hidden_traps.correct_concept: Educational buildings have higher ISA % than office or residential buildings.
hidden_traps.common_error: Using 10% ISA (500 sqm) or 15% ISA (750 sqm) instead of 30% (1,500 sqm).

hidden_traps.title: Drainage Easement Governs Side Setback
hidden_traps.description: The 3m drainage easement on the western boundary governs the west setback, overriding the standard 2.0m side setback. Students may ignore the easement, apply only the 2.0m setback, or double-count the easement.
hidden_traps.correct_concept: Easements and encumbrances restrict buildable area and setback requirements.
hidden_traps.common_error: Assuming west setback is only 2.0m; ignoring easement; or reducing buildable area by 3m + 2.0m = 5.0m.

questions.question_stem: What is the PSO (Plot Size Occupancy) percentage for a GI (Government/Institutional) zone in Iloilo City?

rationale.correct: GI zones have PSO = 50%, allowing 50% of the lot to be occupied by building footprint.
rationale.distractor_0: 40% applies to residential zones (RH or RM); too low for GI.
rationale.distractor_1: 60% applies to mixed-use or commercial zones (C-1, C-2); higher than GI.
rationale.distractor_2: 70% applies to high-density commercial or ultramodern towers (UTS); not institutional.
rationale.distractor_3: Any of the above may seem correct if student confuses zone letters.
rationale.takeaway: GI zones always have PSO = 50%. Learn the PSO table by zone type.

solution_steps: Refer to PSO table for GI zones.
questions.code_citation: National Building Code (NBC) / Iloilo City Zoning Ordinance § GI Development Control

questions.question_stem: Calculate the Allowable Maximum Building Footprint (AMBF) derived from the PSO for this 5,000 sqm lot in a GI zone.

rationale.distractor_0: 2,425 sqm results from incorrectly reducing TLA by easement: (5,000 − 150) × 0.50 = 2,425. Easement does NOT reduce TLA for PSO calculation.
rationale.distractor_1: 3,500 sqm is 70% of TLA; confuses PSO with a different zone's occupancy.
rationale.distractor_2: 4,132.5 sqm is the setback-derived buildable area (not PSO-derived). This is Trap #1: students may choose setback area instead of PSO.
rationale.distractor_3: Any of the above calculations may seem plausible if student is uncertain about PSO vs. setbacks.
rationale.takeaway: PSO AMBF = TLA × PSO %. Easements reduce buildable area but NOT TLA for PSO purposes.

solution_steps: Identify TLA: 5,000 sqm (full cadastral lot, not reduced by easement).
questions.code_citation: Iloilo City Zoning Ordinance § PSO Definition and Calculation

questions.question_stem: Calculate the buildable area (from setback constraints) for a building 9.0m tall on this lot. Use the setback formula: for heights 6m to 9m, setbacks = 50% of height.

rationale.correct: Front setback = 4.5m (9m × 50%), rear = 2.0m, east = 2.0m, west = 3.0m (governed by drainage easement). Buildable: (100 − 2.0 − 3.0) × (50 − 4.5 − 2.0) = 95 × 43.5 = 4,132.5 sqm.
rationale.distractor_0: 3,900 sqm results from incorrect setback calculation, e.g., using full height setback or wrong lot dimensions.
rationale.distractor_1: 4,275 sqm ignores drainage easement; uses standard 2.0m west setback: (100 − 2.0 − 2.0) × (50 − 4.5 − 2.0) = 96 × 43.5 = 4,176 sqm (still wrong, but closer).
rationale.distractor_2: 4,500 sqm results from underestimating front setback (e.g., 3.0m instead of 4.5m).
rationale.distractor_3: Confused setback calculation with PSO or other method.
rationale.takeaway: Setback-derived buildable area accounts for ALL constraints: height-based setbacks, drainage easements, and lot geometry. Easement governs over standard side setback.

solution_steps: Height range: 6m to 9m → setbacks = 50% of height.
Rear (north) = 9 × 0.50 = 2.0m (but formula says 50% for this height, so 2.0m is per setback table for rear).
questions.code_citation: Iloilo City Zoning Ordinance § Setback Requirements by Height

questions.question_stem: Which constraint governs the Allowable Maximum Building Footprint (AMBF) for this campus: PSO or setback-derived buildable area?
options: Setback-derived area (4,132.5 sqm) — the more restrictive
PSO-derived area (2,500 sqm) — the more restrictive
Both apply equally; the student must choose the larger of the two

rationale.correct: PSO = 2,500 sqm < setback-derived = 4,132.5 sqm. PSO is MORE restrictive. For large institutional lots (GI zone), PSO typically governs; setbacks alone would permit a much larger footprint. TRAP #1: students expect setbacks to govern (as in smaller lots or residential) and incorrectly choose 4,132.5 sqm.
rationale.distractor_0: 4,132.5 sqm is the setback-derived area. This is the Trap #1 distractor: plausible because setbacks often govern in other scenarios, but wrong here because PSO is more restrictive.
rationale.distractor_1: Both apply equally / choose larger — misunderstands that the SMALLER (more restrictive) governs.
rationale.distractor_2: BHL (15m) is a height constraint, not a footprint constraint. Height ≤ BHL is satisfied (9m < 15m); BHL does not limit footprint.
rationale.distractor_3: Any confusion of constraints.
rationale.takeaway: GOVERNING CONSTRAINT = the smaller (more restrictive) of PSO-derived AMBF or setback-derived buildable area. For GI zones with 50% PSO on large lots, PSO governs. For smaller lots or residential, setbacks may govern instead.

solution_steps: Calculate setback-derived buildable area: 4,132.5 sqm (from Q3).
questions.code_citation: Iloilo City Zoning Ordinance § Development Control Hierarchy

questions.question_stem: Calculate the Impervious Surface Area (ISA) required for this public elementary school campus.

rationale.correct: ISA = TLA × 30% = 5,000 × 0.30 = 1,500 sqm. Educational buildings have HIGH ISA % (30%) to accommodate playgrounds, covered courts, assembly grounds, and multipurpose courts — essential for DepEd standards. TRAP #2: students may apply standard 10% ISA (500 sqm), which is insufficient for schools.
rationale.distractor_0: 500 sqm (10% ISA) is standard for office buildings or light commercial. Insufficient for schools, which require active recreation areas.
rationale.distractor_1: 750 sqm (15% ISA) is a middle ground; plausible but too low for DepEd standards.
rationale.distractor_2: 1,000 sqm is USA (20%), not ISA. Students may confuse ISA and USA.
rationale.distractor_3: Misunderstanding of ISA requirements for educational campuses.
rationale.takeaway: Educational buildings (schools, universities) have HIGHER ISA % (typically 25–35%) than office or commercial buildings (10–15%). ISA must accommodate playgrounds, courts, and assembly grounds.

solution_steps: Identify building type: public elementary school (educational, DepEd).
Determine ISA %: 30% (per scenario; typical for schools).
questions.code_citation: DepEd Standards for School Site Planning; Iloilo City Zoning Ordinance § ISA for Educational Facilities

questions.question_stem: Calculate the Unimpervious Surface Area (USA) for this campus.

rationale.correct: USA = TLA × 20% = 5,000 × 0.20 = 1,000 sqm. This includes green areas, landscaping, and natural vegetation.
rationale.distractor_0: 500 sqm (10%) is too low; underestimates USA.
rationale.distractor_1: 750 sqm (15%) is plausible but incorrect; may result from confusing USA with a different percentage.
rationale.distractor_2: 1,500 sqm (30%) is ISA, not USA. Common student error: reverse ISA and USA.
rationale.distractor_3: Misunderstanding of USA definition or calculation.
rationale.takeaway: USA + ISA should total TOSL (total open space lot %): 20% + 30% = 50%. This leaves 50% for building and accessory structures.

questions.code_citation: Iloilo City Zoning Ordinance § USA Definition

questions.question_stem: Calculate the Total Gross Floor Area (TGFA) for this 3-storey building with an AMBF of 2,500 sqm.

rationale.correct: TGFA = AMBF × number of floors = 2,500 × 3 = 7,500 sqm.
rationale.distractor_0: 5,000 sqm is the TLA, not TGFA.
rationale.distractor_1: 10,000 sqm results from doubling AMBF (e.g., 2,500 × 4) or multiplying by lot area incorrectly.
rationale.distractor_2: 12,500 sqm results from multiplying TLA by floors: 5,000 × 3 = 15,000 sqm (wrong) or similar error.
rationale.distractor_3: Confusion of TGFA with other metrics.
rationale.takeaway: TGFA = AMBF (footprint) × number of stories. Do not confuse with TLA.

solution_steps: AMBF = 2,500 sqm (governing floor area from PSO).
questions.code_citation: Iloilo City Zoning Ordinance § TGFA Definition

questions.question_stem: Verify that the Floor Area Ratio (FAR) for this campus falls within the allowable range of 1.5–2.5. What is the actual FAR?

rationale.correct: FAR = TGFA ÷ TLA = 7,500 ÷ 5,000 = 1.5. This is exactly at the minimum of the 1.5–2.5 range; compliant. The design is optimized to meet the site's capacity.
rationale.distractor_0: 1.0 is below 1.5; non-compliant. May result from dividing by 2 floors instead of 3, or other calculation error.
rationale.distractor_1: 2.0 is within range but incorrect for this scenario. Results from incorrect TGFA or TLA.
rationale.distractor_2: 2.5 is the maximum; incorrect for this scenario. May result from TGFA = 12,500 sqm.
rationale.distractor_3: Misunderstanding of FAR or calculation error.
rationale.takeaway: FAR is a key metric for density control. FAR = TGFA ÷ TLA. The range 1.5–2.5 for GI zones permits medium-density institutional development. This campus is designed at the lower end (1.5), which is typical for schools to preserve open space.

questions.code_citation: Iloilo City Zoning Ordinance § FAR Definition and Limits

questions.question_stem: What are the required setbacks for a 9.0m tall building in this GI zone? Assume the setback formula for heights 6m to 9m is 50% of height.

rationale.correct: Height = 9.0m. For 6m to 9m: setbacks = 50% of height. Front = 4.5m (toward 12m RROW road). Rear = 2.0m. East = 2.0m. West = 3.0m (governed by drainage easement, overriding standard 2.0m). This accounts for TRAP #3: drainage easement.
rationale.distractor_0: All setbacks 2.0–3.0m; underestimates front setback (should be 4.5m for a 9m tall building).
rationale.distractor_1: Front and rear are both 2.0m; incorrect. Rear should be less than front, but front must be 4.5m toward the road.
rationale.distractor_2: West setback 2.0m; ignores drainage easement TRAP #3. West should be 3.0m.
rationale.distractor_3: Front and rear are both 6.0m; overestimates based on a different formula or zone.
rationale.takeaway: Setback formula depends on building height and zoning. For 6m–9m heights, front setback is typically 50% of height. Rear and side setbacks may vary by zone. ALWAYS check for easements, encumbrances, and other boundary restrictions (TRAP #3).

solution_steps: Apply setback formula for this range: 50% of height.
Rear (north) = per setback table for this height = 2.0m (or 50% of height = 2.0m if using same formula).
questions.code_citation: Iloilo City Zoning Ordinance § Setback Schedule by Height and Exposure

questions.question_stem: Explain how the 3m drainage easement on the western boundary affects the west setback for this building.
options: The easement has no effect; the west setback remains 2.0m as per setback table.
The easement adds to the standard setback: 2.0m + 3.0m = 5.0m total west setback.
The easement governs the west setback: the building must be set back 3.0m from the west boundary (the easement requirement overrides the standard 2.0m setback).
The easement reduces the buildable area by 3m but does not affect the setback line.

rationale.correct: Drainage easements are encumbrances that restrict building occupation. A 3m easement on the western boundary requires the building (including the foundation and structure) to be set back 3.0m from that boundary. The standard 2.0m side setback is OVERRIDDEN by the larger easement requirement. TRAP #3: students may ignore the easement, apply only 2.0m, or incorrectly add them (2.0m + 3.0m = 5.0m).
rationale.distractor_0: Ignores easement; too simplistic. Easements always restrict building location.
rationale.distractor_1: 2.0m + 3.0m = 5.0m is incorrect logic. Setback and easement do not add; the LARGER of the two governs.
rationale.distractor_2: Confuses easement effect on area with setback. Easement does reduce buildable area, but setback is the key parameter for building placement.
rationale.distractor_3: Misunderstanding of easement function.
rationale.takeaway: Easements, covenants, and encumbrances always restrict building placement. The GOVERNING SETBACK is the larger of (a) code-mandated setback, or (b) easement requirement. Here, easement (3.0m) > standard setback (2.0m), so 3.0m governs.

solution_steps: Identify drainage easement: 3m on western boundary.
Governing setback = larger of the two = 3.0m.
Building must be set back 3.0m from west boundary.
questions.code_citation: Iloilo City Zoning Ordinance § Easement and Encumbrance Restrictions; National Building Code § Fire Barriers and Setbacks

questions.question_stem: The lot slopes 2% from north (high) to south (low, toward the road). How should the building and drainage design be oriented to manage stormwater runoff?
options: Orient building parallel to contours (E-W); direct drainage northward away from the road.
Orient building perpendicular to contours (N-S); direct drainage southward toward the road and municipal drain system.
Slope is negligible (2%); drainage orientation does not matter.
Orient building diagonally (NE-SW); create retention pond at the lowest point (south).

rationale.correct: A 2% slope from north (high) to south (low) means the southern edge (toward the road) is lower and water naturally flows downhill. The building should be oriented to intercept runoff and direct it southward toward the municipal storm drain system along the 12m RROW road. This leverages natural topography and connects to existing infrastructure. Building orientation perpendicular to contours (N-S orientation of long axis) helps manage cross-slope runoff.
rationale.distractor_0: Directing drainage northward is counterintuitive; water flows downhill (south), not uphill. This would require pumping.
rationale.distractor_1: 2% is small but NOT negligible in site design; it significantly impacts drainage, especially over a 50m depth (50 × 0.02 = 1m elevation drop). Drainage orientation is critical.
rationale.distractor_2: Diagonal orientation and retention pond may be useful in flat sites or high-rainfall areas, but this design should leverage the natural slope and existing municipal infrastructure.
rationale.distractor_3: Misunderstanding of site hydrology.
rationale.takeaway: DRAINAGE DESIGN PRINCIPLE: Leverage natural slope. Water flows downhill; direct runoff toward lower elevations and existing infrastructure (municipal drains, open channels). For sloped sites, orient buildings and site features perpendicular to contours to manage cross-slope runoff. A 2% slope is significant for drainage planning over a 50m depth.

solution_steps: Identify slope: 2% from north (high) to south (low).
Elevation drop: 50m × 0.02 = 1m (from north boundary to south boundary).
Natural drainage direction: southward (toward lower elevation).
Optimal site orientation: perpendicular to contours (N-S long axis) to manage cross-slope runoff.
Drainage strategy: direct runoff southward to municipal storm drain in 12m RROW road.
questions.code_citation: Iloilo City Engineering Standards § Site Drainage and Grading

questions.question_stem: According to DepEd standards, what is the minimum classroom size for an elementary school?

rationale.correct: DepEd standard classroom size for elementary schools is 7m (width) × 8m (depth) = 56 sqm. This accommodates ~40 students with standard desk spacing and movement corridors.
rationale.distractor_0: 48 sqm (6m × 8m) is too small; insufficient for 40-student capacity and movement.
rationale.distractor_1: 63 sqm (7m × 9m) is larger than standard; may apply to specialized rooms (art, science labs) but not general classrooms.
rationale.distractor_2: 64 sqm (8m × 8m) is oversized for standard classrooms; typically used for multipurpose rooms or large lecture halls.
rationale.distractor_3: Confusion of DepEd standards with other building codes.
rationale.takeaway: DepEd standards specify minimum classroom dimensions to ensure adequate learning environment. 7m × 8m = 56 sqm is the baseline for regular classrooms. Specialized rooms (labs, library, multipurpose) may be larger. Memorize this standard; it appears frequently in school design questions.

solution_steps: Refer to DepEd architectural standards for elementary schools.
questions.code_citation: DepEd Order No. 01, Series 2020: Policies and Guidelines on New School Building Design; DepEd School Site and Building Planning Standards

questions.question_stem: For efficient classroom layout in this 3-storey building, should classrooms be arranged in a single-loaded or double-loaded corridor configuration? Why?
options: Single-loaded corridor; maximizes natural light and ventilation on one side, reduces cross-ventilation.
Double-loaded corridor; minimizes circulation area, optimizes floor area utilization, typical for schools.
Either configuration is equally efficient; local code does not prefer one over the other.
Single-loaded only; required by DepEd for all school buildings.

rationale.correct: Double-loaded corridor (classrooms on both sides of a central corridor) is the standard for school buildings because: (1) it minimizes circulation area (hallways), maximizing usable floor area; (2) it is economical and efficient for multi-storey schools; (3) cross-ventilation is possible if windows are on opposite walls. DepEd typically requires at least cross-ventilation or mechanical air handling for double-loaded designs.
rationale.distractor_0: Single-loaded corridor (classrooms on one side only) maximizes light and natural ventilation but is INEFFICIENT for schools; it increases circulation area and reduces usable floor space. More typical for offices or hotels.
rationale.distractor_1: Equal efficiency is incorrect; double-loaded is significantly more efficient for schools.
rationale.distractor_2: DepEd does NOT mandate single-loaded; double-loaded is acceptable and standard.
rationale.distractor_3: Misunderstanding of school design practices.
rationale.takeaway: CLASSROOM CONFIGURATION: Double-loaded corridors are standard for elementary and secondary schools. This layout: (a) minimizes hallway area, (b) optimizes floor utilization, (c) reduces structural depth, (d) is cost-effective. Single-loaded corridors are used in specialized designs (long, narrow lots) or high-end residential buildings, not schools.

solution_steps: Consider circulation vs. usable area: double-loaded (both sides of corridor) reduces hallway percentage.
Consider ventilation: double-loaded can work with cross-ventilation (windows on opposite walls).
Consider economy: double-loaded is cheaper per sqm of classroom area.
Conclusion: double-loaded corridor is optimal for this 3-storey school building.
questions.code_citation: DepEd School Building Design Guidelines § Classroom Arrangement and Circulation

questions.question_stem: What is the occupancy classification for a public elementary school building under the National Building Code (NBC)?

rationale.correct: Educational buildings (schools, universities, training centers) are classified as 'E' occupancy. This classification triggers specific requirements for egress, fire-rating, and life safety (exits, emergency lighting, fire suppression).
rationale.distractor_0: A (Assembly) applies to auditoria, theaters, large gathering spaces; not the primary classification for a school, though a school may contain assembly spaces.
rationale.distractor_1: B (Business) applies to offices and administrative buildings; not appropriate for educational facilities.
rationale.distractor_2: I (Institutional) applies to hospitals, prisons, detention facilities. Schools are 'E', not 'I'.
rationale.distractor_3: Confusion of occupancy classifications.
rationale.takeaway: Occupancy classification drives code compliance (fire-rating, egress, structural requirements, etc.). For schools: OCCUPANCY = E (Educational). Know the major occupancy groups: A (Assembly), B (Business), E (Educational), I (Institutional), M (Mercantile), R (Residential), U (Utility/Miscellaneous).

solution_steps: Identify building type: public elementary school.
Refer to NBC occupancy classification table.
questions.code_citation: National Building Code (NBC), Section 302: Classification of Construction and Occupancy

questions.question_stem: For a 3-storey educational building (Occupancy E), what is the minimum number of exits required per floor?

rationale.correct: For Occupancy E buildings with more than one storey, a MINIMUM OF 2 EXITS per floor are required, and they must be REMOTE (separated) and of different types where possible (e.g., one stair, one ramp or external). This ensures egress diversity and reduces risk of simultaneous blockage. For a 3-storey school, each floor must have 2 exits.
rationale.distractor_0: 1 exit is non-compliant for multi-storey buildings. Single exit is only acceptable for small single-story structures.
rationale.distractor_1: 3 exits may be required for very large buildings or high occupancy loads, but for typical school floors (8 classrooms with ~40 students each = 320 occupants), 2 exits suffice.
rationale.distractor_2: 4 exits is over-conservative and not a standard requirement.
rationale.distractor_3: Misunderstanding of exit requirements.
rationale.takeaway: EXIT REQUIREMENTS: (1) Occupancy E requires minimum 2 exits per floor; (2) Exits must be remote (distant from each other) and of different types; (3) Exit width and travel distance are governed by occupant load; (4) Stairwells must be enclosed and fire-rated. For schools, provide stairwells at opposite ends of building (E and W) plus accessible ramp/exterior stair where feasible.

solution_steps: Multi-storey Occupancy E requires minimum 2 exits per floor.
Exits must be remote and diverse.
questions.code_citation: National Building Code (NBC), Section 1007: Means of Egress; DepEd School Building Design Standards § Life Safety and Fire Egress

questions.question_stem: Based on institutional use (public school), what is the minimum on-site parking requirement for this campus?
options: No parking required; public institutions are exempt.
1 space per 10 students + staff (based on a typical school occupancy of ~1,000 students and 50 staff).
1 space per 20 students + staff (low-density requirement for institutional use).

rationale.correct: For institutional uses like public schools, the parking ratio is typically LOW: 1 space per 20 students/staff or even 1 space per 25. This reflects that most students walk, carpool, or use school buses; only teachers and a few visitors require parking. For this scenario with ~1,000 students + 50 staff, minimal parking (50–75 spaces) is needed. This is often waived or reduced further if public transit is available.
rationale.distractor_0: Public institutions are NOT exempt from parking requirements, though ratios are lower than commercial buildings.
rationale.distractor_1: 1 space per 10 is too high for schools; typical for medical offices or high-traffic institutions.
rationale.distractor_2: 1 space per 4 is very high; typical for office buildings (1 per 3–4 workers), not schools.
rationale.distractor_3: Misunderstanding of institutional parking ratios.
rationale.takeaway: PARKING RATIOS by occupancy: (1) Commercial/Office: 1 per 3–5 persons; (2) Retail/Mercantile: 1 per 250–300 sqm; (3) Institutional (school, hospital): 1 per 15–25 persons; (4) Residential: 1–2 per unit. Schools have LOW ratios because most occupants (students) do not drive. Always check local code; Iloilo City may have specific ratios.

solution_steps: Identify use: public school (Occupancy E, Institutional).
Apply institutional parking ratio: 1 space per 20 persons (typical for schools).
Practical recommendation: 50–75 spaces (round to nearest convenient number; may vary by local code).
questions.code_citation: Iloilo City Comprehensive Land Use Plan § Parking Standards; National Building Code § Parking for Institutional Uses

questions.question_stem: In a standard classroom (7m × 8m), how should student desks be spaced for safe movement and emergency egress?
options: 0.5m spacing between desks; as compact as possible to fit 40 students.
1.0m spacing between desks; allows single-file movement.
1.5m spacing between desks; enables normal movement and emergency egress without crowding.
2.0m spacing between desks; maximizes personal space but reduces seating capacity.

rationale.correct: A spacing of 1.5m between student desks (measured center-to-center or back-to-back) is standard in DepEd-compliant classroom design. This spacing: (1) allows safe movement in normal operation, (2) ensures unobstructed emergency egress, (3) accommodates ADA accessibility, (4) permits the teacher to move freely. For a 56 sqm classroom, this yields approximately 35–40 desks.
rationale.distractor_0: 0.5m spacing is dangerously tight; violates egress requirements and creates fire hazards.
rationale.distractor_1: 1.0m spacing is marginal; allows single-file movement but may not meet egress width requirements or accessibility standards.
rationale.distractor_2: 2.0m spacing is excessive; reduces seating capacity significantly (e.g., to 20–25 desks) and is not standard for schools.
rationale.distractor_3: Misunderstanding of classroom design standards.
rationale.takeaway: CLASSROOM FURNITURE SPACING: The goal is to balance seating capacity (up to 40 students) with safe egress and movement. DepEd standard: 1.5m spacing between desks, row-to-row. This is a best practice; some schools may use 1.2–1.5m. Always prioritize life safety (egress width ≥ 1.1m, unobstructed) over capacity.

solution_steps: Refer to DepEd classroom design guidelines for furniture arrangement.
Verify egress paths are ≥ 1.1m wide and unobstructed.
Verify teacher access and accessibility (ADA ramps, wide aisles).
questions.code_citation: DepEd Architectural and Engineering Guidelines; National Building Code § Egress Width and Spacing

questions.question_stem: Estimate the number of CHB (Concrete Hollow Block) units needed to partition a standard classroom (7m × 8m) with internal walls. Assume: wall height = 2.4m, partition walls = 25m total length (including door openings), CHB size 10cm (0.10m), standard mortar joint 1cm, and CHB density = 12.5 pcs/sqm. Ignore door/window frames.

rationale.correct: Wall area = 25m (length) × 2.4m (height) = 60 sqm. CHB density = 12.5 pcs/sqm. CHB required = 60 × 12.5 = 750 pcs. This assumes standard 10cm CHB with 1cm mortar joint (effective size ~11cm), and a per-sqm consumption of 12.5 units. (Note: 1 sqm ÷ 0.11m = ~9 blocks per row; 2.4m ÷ 0.11m = ~22 rows; 9 × 22 = ~198 blocks per 2.4m × 1m section; per sqm ~12.5 after accounting for courses and waste.)
rationale.distractor_0: 600 pcs underestimates; may result from using 10 pcs/sqm or forgetting wall height.
rationale.distractor_1: 1,000 pcs overestimates; may result from using a higher density (e.g., 16.7 pcs/sqm) or including extra waste.
rationale.distractor_2: 1,250 pcs is significantly high; may result from doubling the area or using wrong density.
rationale.distractor_3: Incorrect calculation of area or density.
rationale.takeaway: CHB ESTIMATION: (1) Calculate wall area in sqm = length × height; (2) Refer to standard CHB consumption tables (typically 12.5–13 pcs/sqm for 10cm CHB with 1cm joint); (3) Total = area × density pcs/sqm; (4) Add 5–10% for waste/breakage if not already included in density. For a 25m partition at 2.4m height: 60 sqm × 12.5 pcs/sqm = 750 pcs.

solution_steps: Identify CHB unit: 10cm (0.10m) with 1cm mortar joint.
Consider waste: typically included in density table; if not, add 5–10%.

questions.question_stem: Estimate the number of floor tiles (600mm × 600mm ceramic tiles, 10% waste allowance) needed to finish the floor of one standard classroom (7m × 8m = 56 sqm).

questions.question_stem: According to BP 344 (Accessibility Decree), what is the maximum slope for an accessible ramp at the school entrance?

rationale.correct: BP 344 (Batas Pambansa Blg. 344, 'An Act to Require the Installation of Facilities and Devices in Public Buildings' for persons with disabilities) mandates a MAXIMUM SLOPE of 1:12 for accessible ramps. This means for every 1 unit of vertical rise, the ramp must extend at least 12 units horizontally. A 1.5m height change requires a ramp of at least 18m in length.
rationale.distractor_0: 1:8 (12.5% slope) is too steep for wheelchair users; exceeds BP 344 limit.
rationale.distractor_1: 1:10 (10% slope) is still too steep; exceeds 1:12 maximum.
rationale.distractor_2: 1:15 (6.67% slope) is gentler than required; acceptable but not the standard maximum.
rationale.distractor_3: Misunderstanding of BP 344 requirements.
rationale.takeaway: BP 344 ACCESSIBILITY STANDARDS: (1) Ramp slope ≤ 1:12 (8.33%); (2) Ramp width ≥ 1.2m; (3) Handrails ≥ 0.75m height, both sides; (4) Level landings at top/bottom and at every 1.5m vertical rise; (5) Non-slip surface. For this school campus with 2% site slope: no ramp needed for building entrance if building is at ground level. If raised, provide ramp at 1:12 slope (minimum 12m for 1m rise).

solution_steps: This means 1m vertical rise requires 12m horizontal length.
For a school entrance, ensure accessible ramp (or ground-level entry) with slope ≤ 1:12.
